title: A Look at Social Media and Misinformation in Regard to Abortion [ID: 1379920]
screen_reason: Conference-abstract content analysis of scraped Instagram posts carrying abortion hashtags, coded for presence and accuracy of medical content: 'Of posts containing medical information, 63.5% were accurate, and 36.5% contained misinformation.' That is a share of items classified inaccurate with an identified (if unquantified) denominator - a CONTENT prevalence estimate. Only the abstract is available, so the sample size, coding rubric, coder count and reliability are unknown.

estimates.country: Not stated (abstract gives no country; hashtags are English-language and the topic is the abortion pill in Jan-Jul 2022, published in an American obstetrics/gynecology abstract supplement)
estimates.measure_type: % of Instagram abortion-hashtag posts containing medical information that contained medical misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 63.5% were accurate, and 36.5% contained misinformation (of posts containing medical information; counts not reported)
estimates.denominator: Instagram posts CONTAINING MEDICAL INFORMATION, drawn from open-source posts scraped with a web-scraper program that had >=250 likes, were posted 1 January-11 July 2022 and contained at least one of #AbortionPill, #AbortionFacts or #UnplannedPregnancy; neither the number of scraped posts nor the number containing medical information is reported
estimates.definition: Post coded as containing misinformation when its medical content was judged inaccurate ('Posts were analyzed for poster self-identification as a physician, nonphysician provider, or nonmedical provider and for presence and accuracy of medical content'); the accuracy standard, rubric and reference sources are not stated in the abstract
estimates.misinfo_def: No definition given. The abstract's only framing is: "Our study aimed to define the rate of medical misinformation for abortion on Instagram and evaluate its source."
estimates.n: not reported (posts containing medical information; total scraped posts also not reported)
estimates.source_quote: Of posts containing medical information, 63.5% were accurate, and 36.5% contained misinformation.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NOT REPORTED in the abstract: no reference standard (guideline, fact-check or expert panel) is named, the number of coders is not given, and no inter-rater reliability statistic is provided. Coding is presumed to be by the study team ('Posts were analyzed ... for presence and accuracy of medical content').
estimates.moderator_quote: Open-source posts through the platform Instagram were collected using a web-scraper program. Posts met the following preset parameters; greater than or equal to 250 likes, posted January 1, 2022 to July 11, 2022, and containing at least one prespecified hashtag: #AbortionPill, #AbortionFacts, #UnplannedPregnancy.
estimates.notes: confidence=low: abstract only. Three material unknowns - (i) no denominator count at any stage, so the estimate cannot be weighted or checked; (ii) no accuracy rubric or reference standard, so the 36.5% rests on unspecified judgement; (iii) the denominator is the SUBSET of posts 'containing medical information', not all scraped posts, so this is not the share of abortion-hashtag posts that are misinformation - the share over all posts would be lower and is not derivable. denom_selection=curated: posts were filtered to >=250 likes, an engagement threshold that selects popular posts, on top of a three-hashtag frame. breadth=false ('inaccurate' medical content) is inferred from the accuracy framing; 'misleading' would be defensible since no rubric distinguishes false from misleading claims.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) '97% of posts were from nonmedical providers, 1.5% from physicians and 1.5% from nonphysician providers' - poster-type composition of the whole sample, not a misinformation share. (2) 'Seventy-nine percent of posts with inaccurate information were from nonmedical providers, 10.5% from physicians, and 10.5% from nonphysician providers' - the denominator is the misinformation posts, so this is composition OF misinformation by source, the wrong denominator direction for prevalence (the useful figure, the share of nonmedical-provider posts that were inaccurate, is not derivable without counts). (3) '47.9% of all posts were pro-abortion, 34.8% were anti-abortion, and 17.3% took no stance' - stance composition, not veracity. (4) 'Of posts containing medical misinformation, 84.2% were anti-abortion, and 15.8%, pro-abortion' - within-misinformation composition by stance; interesting for interpretation but not a prevalence share. Nothing else in the abstract is quantitative. Flags for the adjudicator: no country is stated (coded Global/global, though the context strongly implies the United States); the denominator is the medical-information subset rather than all posts; and if the project's convention is to require a reported denominator SIZE, this row would fail that test - the value itself is verbatim and R8-clean, but n is unknown.

rob.design: Cross-sectional Instagram content analysis reported as a conference abstract (about 250 words); posts collected with a web-scraper under preset parameters (>=250 likes; posted 1 Jan-11 Jul 2022; at least one of #AbortionPill, #AbortionFacts, #UnplannedPregnancy); each post coded for poster type (physician / nonphysician provider / nonmedical provider), presence and accuracy of medical content, and abortion stance. NO sample size at any stage, NO accuracy rubric or reference standard, NO statement of how many coders judged accuracy, NO reliability statistic, and no full-text methods available. The >=250-like threshold makes the sample engagement-selected rather than representative of abortion-hashtag posts.
rob.item6_quote: Posts were analyzed for poster self-identification as a physician, nonphysician provider, or nonmedical provider and for presence and accuracy of medical content.
rob.item10_quote: Of posts containing medical information, 63.5% were accurate, and 36.5% contained misinformation.
